senses: Not in accordance with good policy.
ety: From im- + politic.
examples: And thereafter it became impolitic to say anything critical about the Harris sprint.

senses: In Russia, the head man of a village community.
In the former kingdom of Poland, a noble holding a castle and domain bestowed by the Crown.
ety: From Russian ста́роста (stárosta) and Polish starosta, both ultimately from Proto-Slavic *starosta, from *starostь (“old age”) + *-a (suffix forming agent nouns).
examples: One family, whose chief…performs the functions of staroste, or magistrate of the village.
Their elders, whom they still…style Starosts.
They…are governed by their own elders or starosti.

senses: Forgetfulness of the past; oblivion.
Dissimulation.
ety: From Latin Lēthē, from Ancient Greek Λήθη (Lḗthē, “forgetfulness”).
examples: What does it mean to say that the stream of silence originates in lethe? It means, above all, that the stream has its source (Quelle) in that which has not yet been said and which must remain unsaid: the "unsaid."

senses: The planet Venus as the morning star.
ety: From Middle English daysterre, from Old English dæġsteorra, equivalent to day + star. Cognate with Scots daystern (“morningstar; daystar”).
examples: Here dawn'd the daystar of Hesperia's fame, / Here herald glory first emblazed her name;
And we have more sure the prophetic word; to which ye do well that ye take heed, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the daystar arise in your hearts;

senses: To discourage, intimidate.
To overwhelm.
ety: From Middle English daunten, from Old French danter, donter (“to tame”), from Latin domitō (“tame”, verb), frequentative of Latin domō (“tame, conquer”, verb), from Proto-Italic *domaō, from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂- (“to domesticate, tame”). Doublet of dompt.
examples: No, I shall not disgrace the Cause, I shall not grieve my comrades by weak surrender! I will fight and struggle, and not be daunted by threat or torture.
Ah, I have changed, I do not know Why lonely hours affect me so. In days of yore, this were not wont, No loneliness my soul could daunt.

senses: An interpretive commentary on scripture, especially one in Hebrew.
ety: Transliteration of Hebrew פֵּשֶׁר (pēšer, “interpretation, solution”). Popularised after the discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls in 1947.
examples: Of all the Dead Sea texts it is the Habakkuk pesher (1QpHab) that, by common consent, exhibits the most impressive agreements with a Targum text.
The Pesher on Zephaniah (1Q15)⁴⁵ interprets Zeph 1:18 and 2:2 as referring to "all the inhabitants of the Land of Judah" (i.5).
According to the suggested interpretation he sinned horribly; his victims were 'only' Pharisees, but the author of the pesher does think that he went too far in his tyrannical actions.

senses: Accompanied with hisses.
Making a hissing sound.
Childish or petulant.
ety: From hiss + -y.
examples: Midwestern-bred and still wholesome despite his exposure to New York’s hissiest, Sam remains the play’s anchor.

senses: To make someone or something immune to something.
ety: From French immuniser, equivalent to immune + -ize.
examples: It is now clear that the brevity of an indecent broadcast – be it word or image – cannot immunize it from FCC censure.

senses: A bulk mass, usually of small items, particularly money; a wad
ety: Probably an alteration of wedge. Compare wad.
examples: He paid a wodge of dosh for his new motor from the car dealership.
I lifted the lid off the second tureen and uncovered a wodge of macaroni, stone-cold and stuck together in a gluey paste.
Bad food, bad drinks, no decent pubs, no laughter in public, and dodgy money-changers hissing that communism was shit and who then disappeared, leaving us with wodges of worthless notes.

senses: glowing; radiant
ety: From a- + glow.
examples: My prayer is a rapture in blue With a world far away And your lips close to mine Tonight while our hearts are aglow Oh, tell me the words I am longing to know
The fall wind stirs and the earth is aglow. Everything is golden.
Kabul skies were aglow with fireworks as Afghans celebrated stunning Cricket World Cup victory over Pakistan.

senses: Something resembling honeycomb (noun sense 1) in having numerous cells or small holes.
Something resembling honeycomb in sweetness; hence, something desirable or pleasant.
A crumbly confection usually made by boiling together golden syrup, sugar, bicarbonate of soda, and water.
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English honycomb, from Old English huniġcamb, from huniġ (“honey”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kn̥h₂ónks (“honey”)) + camb (“comb”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“peg; tooth; row of teeth”)). The English word is analysable as honey + comb. The Oxford English Dictionary posits that the arrangement of several plates of wax “hanging parallel to each other from the roof of the hive suggests a comb with its teeth”. The verb is derived from the noun. Compare Saterland Frisian Hunichmoarte (“honeycomb”), West Frisian huningskiif (“honeycomb”)
examples: The wood porch was a honeycomb of termite tunnels before we replaced it.
Yes, Frank, what I have is my own, if labour in getting, and care in augmenting, can make a right of property; and no drone shall feed on my honeycomb.

senses: Either rear half of a side of beef, mutton, veal, lamb or by extension from another edible mammal.
The hind biped (leg) of a quadruped, or all body parts situated behind the hind legs' trunk-attachment.
ety: From hind + quarter.
examples: While Major was speaking four large rats had crept out of their holes and were sitting on their hindquarters, listening to him.

senses: The dignity and ecclesiastic office of Roman Catholic cardinal.
The Roman Catholic cardinals, taken collectively.
ety: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin cardinālātus, from cardinālis (“cardinal”) + -ātus, itself the noun use of an adjective derived from cardō (“hinge, main point”) + -ālis (“-al”). By surface analysis, cardinal + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).
examples: The cardinalate ranks equal to a secular prince of the blood.
The cardinalate under a maximum age composes the conclave which elects the pope.

senses: To separate one substance from another by means of a solvent; to wash; to cleanse.
ety: First attested in 1731. Borrowed from Latin ēlūtus, from the verb ēluō (“to wash away”).
examples: A mixture of isooctane and ethyl acetate can be used to elute triglycerides from a complex lipid solution.

senses: A share or portion, especially a smaller share.
Each descent group in a culture which is divided exactly into two descent groups.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French moytié, from Old French meitié (“half”) (modern French moitié (“half”)), from Late Latin medietās (“centre, midpoint; half”), from Latin medius (“half; middle”) + -tās (from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being)). Medius is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle”), possibly from *me-dʰi- (“among; with”), from *me (“in the middle of; among; with”). The word is a doublet of mediety.
examples: Arrangements were made with the B. & M.R., however, whereby the latter took over the Machen Loop in consideration for granting the P.C. & N.R. a moiety of the earnings of the Caerphilly branch.

senses: From or evoking the first decade of a century (chiefly the 2000s).
ety: From the sense of aught to refer to the number zero.
examples: Meyer and his team collected the participants in a very aughts way — through Craigslist.
He's testing out new experiments with knotting and macramé too, tying up dresses and trousers for a look that feels very aughts—and very now.

senses: The withdrawal of one's senses; focus on oneself as opposed to external stimuli.
ety: From Sanskrit प्रत्याहार (pratyāhāra, “withdrawal”).
examples: By withdrawing our awareness from negative impressions, pratyahara strengthens the mind's powers of immunity.

senses: A type of Mexican horseman.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish charro (“cowboy”).
examples: The star is Jorge Negrete, a tall baritone with a pencil mustache who appeared as a singing charro in a few dozen ranchero musicals.
But he's also evolved from the mythic Mexican cowboy of the 19th century, the charro, who even if he had nothing else had balls.

senses: Imperfect, makeshift; ramshackle, second-rate.
Built from natural materials, especially unfired mud and thatch.
ety: From Hindi कच्चा (kaccā, “raw, unripe”).
examples: The manager publicly announced that the kutcha house loan was for those who lived in thatched huts and the linkage loan for those who lived in tiled houses!

senses: Focused on the phallus, especially as a symbol of male dominance; characterised by male attitudes, focused on men.
ety: From phallo- + -centric.
examples: His shame at what she might on the other hand perceive as his slimy phallocentric conduct toward her made it easier for him to avoid her, as well.

senses: Commonwealth standard spelling of satirize.
ety: From satire + -ise.
examples: The singer was satirised during the episode Panic on the Streets of Springfield, which aired in the US on Sunday night.

senses: Carnegiea gigantea, a large cactus native to the Sonoran Desert and characterized by its "arms".
ety: From Mexican Spanish saguaro, from a Taracahitic Uto-Aztecan language, probably Yaqui, Mayo or Opata.
examples: The Suwarrow or Saguaro of the natives.
The Pitella (pronounced Pitayo) and the Saguaro are the most prized.

senses: A straw rope.
A blanket or bedroll used for camping out.
ety: Borrowed from Irish súgán (“rope”), from Proto-Celtic *souggo, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“to bend, to cut, to drive”), see also Sanskrit सुवति (suvati). Doublet of soogan.
examples: Lead him home with a sugan the way you’d lead a bleating goat.

senses: Serving to fill up, merely for effect, otherwise redundant.
Marked by expletives (phrase-fillers).
ety: From Late Latin explētīvus (“serving to fill out”), from Latin explētus, the perfect passive participle of expleō (“fill out”), itself from ex (“out, completely”) + *pleō (“fill”).
examples: No one entered more fully than Shakespeare into the character of this species of poetry, which admits of no expletive imagery, no merely ornamental line.

senses: A Persian money of account or gold coin issued until 1927, notionally worth 10,000 dinars.
An Iranian coin or value of 10 rials.
ety: Borrowed from Classical Persian تومان (tōman), from Mongolian түмэн (tümen).
examples: The band-roll strung with tomans Which proves the veil a Persian woman's

senses: The art or pseudoscience of deducing the predominant temper and other characteristic qualities of the mind from the outward appearance, especially from the features of the face.
The face or countenance, with respect to the temper of the mind; particular configuration, cast, or expression of countenance, as denoting character.
The art of telling fortunes by inspection of the features.
The general appearance or aspect of a thing, without reference to its scientific characteristics.
ety: Inherited from Middle English phisonomie, from Anglo-Norman phisenomie, Middle French phisonomie et al., ultimately from Late Latin physiognomia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμία (phusiognōmía, “physiology”), from φύσις (phúsis, “physique, appearance”) + γνώμη (gnṓmē, “means of knowing”). Middle English phisonomie would regularly develop into *physnomy /ˈfɪznəmi/ (forms of this type are common in Early Modern English, such as fisnomie in All's Well that Ends Well); the modern spelling and pronunciation are due to learned influence.
examples: During a period of peak popularity in the 19ᵗʰ Century, the field of physiognomy became more sinister and racist than its quirky manifestation during the time of ancient Greeks.

senses: A person who makes ceramics objects; a potter.
ety: From ceram(ic) + -ist.
examples: The Corfu, Greece-born, London-based ceramist Agalis Manessi, 69, creates her animals — recumbent hounds, alert hares — from lumps of terra-cotta clay that she squeezes and manipulates “until a figure emerges.”

senses: Having a buzzing sound.
Being the subject of cultural buzz.
Using a large number of buzzwords.
ety: From buzz + -y.
examples: Collins shifts the slide, and the trumpet phrase gets faster and faster until it blurs into a buzzy pitch.
This time, my host asked me if I was part of LinkedIn, a buzzy Web site intended to link people with similar business interests.

One afternoon in June, I was out with a stranger at my local park. The algorithms recommended we meet. He told me he had been reading How to Do Nothing: Resisting the Attention Economy, a buzzy bestseller by Jenny Odell.

senses: An organism that feeds chiefly on animals; an animal that feeds on meat as the main part of its diet.
A person who is not a vegetarian.
A follower of the carnivore diet.
ety: Borrowed from French carnivore, from Latin carnivorus. In the zoological sense, coined by William Whewell in 1840 as an adaptation of Cuvier's coinage, French carnivore.
examples: As juveniles the crocodiles are frequently predated by larger carnivores.
Well, she has now gone / From this unhappy planet / With all the carnivores / And the destructors on it

senses: A trunk (boot, storage compartment) located at the front rather than the rear of a car.
ety: Blend of front + trunk.
examples: The Model S, showing off both its traditional trunk and its surprising "frunk."

senses: The dried rhizome and roots of Rheum palmatum (Chinese rhubarb) or Rheum officinale (Tibetan rhubarb), from China, used as a laxative and purgative.
A ditch alongside a road or highway.
ety: From Middle English rubarbe, from Anglo-Norman reubarbe (modern French rhubarbe), from Late Latin reubarbarum, rheubarbarum, rubarbera, rybarba, probably from Koine Greek ῥῆον βαρβαρικόν (rhêon barbarikón), from ῥῆον (rhêon, “rhubarb”) + Ancient Greek βαρβαρικόν (barbarikón), neuter of βαρβαρικός (barbarikós, “foreign; barbaric”) (English barbaric). There is also a Medieval Latin variant rabarbarum, which appears to be influenced by Ancient Greek ῥᾶ (rhâ, “rhubarb”), and gave rise to some of the forms in modern languages. The Ancient Greek variant term appears to have been folk-etymologically
examples: Driving home yesterday, I almost hit the rhubarb.

senses: Characterized or marked by meddling; inclined or having a tendency to meddle or interfere in other people's business.
ety: From meddle + -some.
examples: If those meddlesome kids hadn't turned me in, I'd have gotten away with my nefarious scheme!
As this was well before the meddlesome days in which we now live, can Mr. Cox explain why this plan was never carried out?
The help tended to be officious, the rules, if heeded, restrictive, and the management meddlesome.

senses: A region or sovereign nation headed by a prince or princess.
ety: From Middle English principalte, principalite, from Anglo-Norman principalté, Middle French principalté, from Late Latin prīncipālitās, from Latin prīncipālis (“principal”) + -tās. Equivalent to principal + -ity.
examples: At this time Russia consisted of a dozen or so principalities, which were frequently at war with one another.
The principality of Freedonia (www.freedonia.org), an earnest collective of secessionist superlibertarians based in Boston, falls into the first category.

senses: Cute, adorable.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 可愛(かわい)い (kawaii, “lovable; adorable; cute”).
examples: She bought a kawaii keychain shaped like a kitten.

senses: Extremely sour, bitter.
Sharp, caustic, severe.
Causing a dry or puckering mouthfeel; characteristic of foods with high tannin content, such as certain kinds of berries and citrus fruits.
ety: From Latin adstringere (“to bind fast”), from ad (“toward”) + stringere (“bind, pull tight”). Compare stringent.
examples: Philip, who was made Duke of Edinburgh on the couple’s wedding, introduced a new, less stuffy, though as the years went on occasionally astringent, tone to the royal family.

senses: A kind of blood sausage in French, Belgian, Luxembourgish and related cuisines.
A sausage in southern Louisiana Creole and Cajun cuisine, made from rice, ground pork (occasionally crawfish), and spices in a sausage casing.
A structure formed by boudinage: one or a series of elongated, sausage-shaped section(s) in rock.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French boudin. Doublet of pudding. Cf. also poutine.
examples: Eurohucksters will find it difficult to wean the sausage lovers of Liége away from their bursting black Belgian boudins and toward Birmingham's humble bangers. Beer hawkers should fare no better.
In general the softer, mousse-like texture of French boudins is the more appropriate in this instance.
Small bodies of mafic to ultramafic rocks occur as boudins or sills up to 7 km long within the gneiss.

senses: Vindictive or wanting vengeance.
ety: From venge + -ful.
examples: His chains now broken, the prisoner turned a vengeful eye toward his former captors.
A vengeful mother-of-three has been jailed for 168 days after being convicted of killing a neighbour's kitten by microwaving the 10-week-old pet.

senses: The biological drive to preserve oneself; love of life.
The love of or empathy with nature and all living things.
ety: From bio- + -philia.
examples: Biophilia (βίος, life; φιλία, love). The instinct of self-preservation common to man and the lower animals.

senses: A Mexican dish of cornmeal dough shell filled with various ingredients (e.g. chopped beef, pork, sweet filling) then steamed in corn husks.
ety: Back-formation from the plural tamales, derived from Latin American Spanish tamales, plural of tamal, derived from Nahuatl tamalli (“wrapped”), derived from Proto-Uto-Aztecan *tïmaL-. Compare O'odham cemait (“tortilla”), Hopi tuma (“stone griddle for cooking corn flatbread”), Ute tʉ'ma- (“to roast under ashes”).
examples: She would peel back the husk, ladle over the salsa verde, stab a plastic fork straight down into the heart of the masa, and hand the tamale over to me.

senses: A topless female street performer covered in body paint who poses for photographs in exchange for tips in the pedestrian plaza of New York City's Times Square.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish desnuda, the feminine singular of desnudo (“naked, nude, undressed”), ultimately from Latin nūdus (“naked, nude, undressed”) and Proto-Indo-European *negʷ- (“bare, naked”).
examples: Muslims, and a number of Americans alike, would be alarmed with some of the street performers found in New York's Times Square, especially the daily routine of desnudas.
